amazing-grace.text: These words were first printed in 1779, in Olney Hymns, a hymnbook made in an English village with the poet William Cowper. Their title there was Faith's Review and Expectation.
The tune uses only five different notes, a pentatonic scale. Moved to F sharp major, all five are black keys on a piano.
amazing-grace.source: The tune's own notes (G, A, B, D and E)

amazing-grace.text: The tune, now called New Britain, survives from 1828 on the back of a letter, and was printed in 1829 in Columbian Harmony, a shape-note book whose notes have shapes that show their place in the scale.

The verse about ten thousand years, often sung last, isn't from the 1779 words: it comes from a 1790 hymn collection. Harriet Beecher Stowe printed it with Amazing Grace in Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852), and no hymnal paired them until 1909.

happy-birthday.text: The tune began as Good Morning to All, a song to start the school day, printed in 1893 in Song Stories for the Kindergarten by two sisters, Mildred and Patty Hill.
happy-birthday.source: Wikipedia, "Happy Birthday to You", its origins

happy-birthday.text: For decades a music publisher was paid whenever the song was sung in a film or on television. In 2015 a US federal court ruled that it held no valid copyright in the words.
happy-birthday.source: Marya v. Warner/Chappell Music (US District Court, Central District of California, 2015); Wikipedia, "Happy Birthday to You", its copyright

happy-birthday.text: In the European Union, the copyright in the words ran out at the end of 2016, seventy years after Patty Hill died.
happy-birthday.source: Wikipedia, "Happy Birthday to You", its copyright

happy-birthday.text: The 1998 Guinness Book of World Records named it the most recognised song in the English language.

michael-row.text: A 1960 recording by the Highwaymen, a folk group formed by college students, went to number one in the United States and in Britain in 1961.
michael-row.source: Wikipedia, "Michael, Row the Boat Ashore", its recordings

michael-row.text: The Michael of the song is usually taken to be the archangel Michael.

are-you-sleeping.text: In the original words, the sleeping brother is late to ring the bells for matins, the early morning prayers, and the ding, dang, dong is those bells.

silent-night.text: Mohr asked Gruber for music for two solo voices and choir, with guitar, and the carol was first sung that way at Christmas Eve Mass in 1818.
Mohr wrote six verses. The English most people sing, John Freeman Young's from 1859, keeps just three of them: the first, the sixth and the second.
Its first printing, around 1833 in Dresden, was among four 'genuine Tyrolean songs' sung by the Strassers, a travelling family of singers who also made gloves.
Gruber's original was a moderate tune in 6/8 with the rocking lilt of a siciliana. The melody sung today differs from it slightly, most of all in the last phrase.

auld-lang-syne.text: Burns's words were first printed in 1796 to a slow, haunting tune. The tune we sing joined them in 1799, in George Thomson's collection of Scottish airs.
auld-lang-syne.source: The Conversation (Kirsteen McCue, University of Glasgow), "How Auld Lang Syne switched tunes en route to world domination"

auld-lang-syne.text: At Hogmanay in Scotland, people cross their arms and join hands with the neighbours on each side as the last verse begins, rather than from the first line.
Burns said the song was old and had never been printed or even written down until he took it down from an old man's singing.
auld-lang-syne.source: Library of Congress, Folklife Today, "Auld Acquaintance for the New Year: Burns's Auld Lang Syne"

auld-lang-syne.text: Burns didn't begin from nothing: several lines of his earliest version match an older song printed in 1711, in James Watson's Choice Collection of Scots Poems.
auld-lang-syne.source: Library of Congress, Folklife Today, "Auld Acquaintance for the New Year: Burns's Auld Lang Syne"

auld-lang-syne.text: In Japan the tune carries other words, Hotaru no Hikari, first printed in an 1881 school songbook. Shops and restaurants play it at closing time to see customers out.

be-thou-my-vision.text: The Irish poem is sometimes credited to a saint of the 500s, but its language points to the 10th or 11th century. Its oldest surviving copies date from the 1400s or 1500s.
The tune is an Irish folk melody. In Patrick Joyce's 1909 collection of old Irish folk music it went with a love song, With My Love on the Road.
A hymnal handbook praises the tune's wide-ranging phrases, and says its usual harmony suits good singers, especially low basses.
be-thou-my-vision.source: Hymnary.org, "SLANE" (tune notes from the Psalter Hymnal Handbook, 1988)

be-thou-my-vision.text: The same tune carries another hymn, Lord of All Hopefulness, first printed with it in 1931. Its writer, Jan Struther, is best known in England for her novel Mrs Miniver.
be-thou-my-vision.source: Hymnary.org, "Lord of all hopefulness, Lord of all joy"

shenandoah.text: At sea it became a capstan shanty: sailors sang it while turning the capstan, a big upright winch, to haul in the anchor.
In some old versions Shenandoah is a man, not a river: an Oneida chief, whose daughter a trader falls in love with.
The shanty collector Richard Runciman Terry wrote that every sailor he met knew it, yet no two sang it quite alike, and that it was always sung with deep feeling, in a very free rhythm.
shenandoah.source: Mainly Norfolk, "Shenandoah" (Martyn Wyndham-Read song notes, quoting Terry)

o-come-all-ye-faithful.text: John Francis Wade earned his living copying and selling plainchant and other music by hand. The hymn survives in several manuscripts he signed.
In London it caught on at the Portuguese embassy chapel, where Samuel Webbe was organist. Sheet music of about 1799 sold it as the favourite Portuguese hymn.
Frederick Oakeley's English version of about 1841 began with a different line. The opening everyone sings now came from a reworking in an 1852 hymnal.
The Latin hymn grew to eight verses: Wade's four, three by Borderies printed in 1822, and an anonymous one from 1857. An 1884 hymnal made the first real try at all eight in English.

ode-to-joy.text: Listen near the end: Beethoven's tune pushes in early, with an accent just before the last phrase. Many hymnals flatten it, squaring that line up on the beat.
ode-to-joy.source: Hymnology Archive, "Joyful, Joyful, We Adore Thee"

ode-to-joy.text: On Christmas Day 1989, weeks after the Berlin Wall opened, Leonard Bernstein conducted it in Berlin with players from Dresden, Leningrad, London, New York and Paris, the chorus singing Freiheit (freedom) for Freude (joy).
ode-to-joy.source: Leonard Bernstein Office, "Berlin Wall (1989)", Historic Concerts

ode-to-joy.text: Schiller wrote the poem in the summer of 1785, and it appeared the next year in the German magazine Thalia. Beethoven's sung text isn't all Schiller: it adds lines of his own.
In a 1907 letter, Henry van Dyke said he wrote these words with Beethoven's music always in his head, and gave the melody the credit for whatever was good in them.
ode-to-joy.source: Hymnology Archive, "Joyful, Joyful, We Adore Thee"

ode-to-joy.text: In 1846 Elam Ives printed the melody as a hymn tune called Bonn, adding a pickup note before every phrase to fit the words.
ode-to-joy.source: Hymnology Archive, "Joyful, Joyful, We Adore Thee"

row-row-row.text: Today's tune appears in the Franklin Square Song Collection of 1881, a songbook for schools and homes, printed as a round and credited to E. O. Lyte.
row-row-row.source: Internet Archive, "Franklin Square Song Collection" (J. P. McCaskey, Harper & Brothers), "Row Your Boat (Round)"

row-row-row.text: Leave out the quick passing notes and every note of the tune belongs to one chord, the home chord. That's why it makes such an easy round: any voice fits any other.
row-row-row.source: The song's own chords (one chord, C, throughout); Wikipedia, "Round (music)"

shchedryk.text: Shchedryk is built on an ostinato: one short four-note figure that keeps repeating while the other voices build around it.
shchedryk.source: America Magazine (Jim McDermott, 2022), "The story of 'Carol of the Bells,' a Christmas classic born in Ukraine"

shchedryk.text: In Shchedryk's Ukrainian words, a swallow flies into a household and tells the family how rich their coming year will be.
shchedryk.source: The song's own words (a shchedrivka, a New Year's well-wishing song); Interlude, "Carol of the Bells by Mykola Leontovych: History and Recordings"

shchedryk.text: The same chorus sang Shchedryk at Carnegie Hall on 5 October 1922, its first performance in the United States.
shchedryk.source: America Magazine (Jim McDermott, 2022), "The story of 'Carol of the Bells,' a Christmas classic born in Ukraine"

shchedryk.text: Oleksander Koshyts's Ukrainian National Chorus carried Shchedryk abroad, giving hundreds of concerts in 45 cities across 10 European countries in two years.
shchedryk.source: America Magazine (Jim McDermott, 2022), "The story of 'Carol of the Bells,' a Christmas classic born in Ukraine"

shchedryk.text: Shchedryk is one of more than 150 choral pieces Leontovych made from Ukrainian folk songs, and by far the best known.
shchedryk.source: Encyclopedia of Ukraine (Canadian Institute of Ukrainian Studies), "Leontovych, Mykola"

simple-gifts.text: Shaker manuscripts also call it Dancing Song or Quick Dance. It was meant to go fast, and the words of its second half, about bowing, bending and turning, were dance directions.
simple-gifts.source: American Music Preservation (Roger Lee Hall), "Joseph Brackett's 'Simple Gifts': Shaker simplicity in song"

simple-gifts.text: Sydney Carter's 1963 hymn Lord of the Dance is sung to this tune, so hymnals print the melody with his words as well as the original Shaker ones.
simple-gifts.source: Hymnary.org, "Lord of the Dance" (text) and "SIMPLE GIFTS" (tune)

simple-gifts.text: In 1950 Copland also arranged it for voice and piano, in his first set of Old American Songs. Peter Pears and Benjamin Britten gave the first performance, at Aldeburgh in England.
simple-gifts.source: IRCAM, Brahms database, "Old American Songs I (1950)"

swing-low.text: The melody is pentatonic, made from just five notes, and built for call and response: a soloist sings the verses while the group answers with the repeated lines.
swing-low.source: Hymnology Archive (Chris Fenner), "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot"

swing-low.text: The oldest known recording of it is a wax cylinder made in 1894 by the Standard Quartette, an African American vocal group.
An 1874 book, Hampton and Its Students, printed it with a very different melody, one that is also pentatonic.
swing-low.source: Hymnology Archive (Chris Fenner), "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot"

swing-low.text: In 1917 Harry T. Burleigh arranged it as a concert song for solo voice and piano, published by G. Ricordi.
swing-low.source: Hymnology Archive (Chris Fenner), "Swing Low, Sweet Chariot"

swing-low.text: In 2011 Oklahoma made it the state's official gospel song.
swing-low.source: State Symbols USA, "Oklahoma State Gospel Song: 'Swing Low, Sweet Chariot' by Wallis Willis"

red-river-valley.text: The oldest known written copy of the words is a manuscript found in Iowa, marked with the year 1879.
red-river-valley.source: Manitoba Historical Society, Manitoba History no. 72 (2013), James J. Nystrom, "The True Story of the Song 'Red River Valley'"

red-river-valley.text: Carl T. Sprague recorded it in 1925 under another name, Cowboy Love Song. A 1927 record by Hugh Cross and Riley Puckett became the cowboy version's biggest hit.
red-river-valley.source: Manitoba Historical Society, Manitoba History no. 72 (2013), James J. Nystrom, "The True Story of the Song 'Red River Valley'"

red-river-valley.text: The folklorist Edith Fowke called it probably the best known folk song on the Canadian prairies.
red-river-valley.source: Manitoba Historical Society, Manitoba History no. 72 (2013), James J. Nystrom, "The True Story of the Song 'Red River Valley'"

red-river-valley.text: It is the official slow march of the Fort Garry Horse, a Canadian Army regiment based in Winnipeg.
red-river-valley.source: Government of Canada, National Defence, "The Fort Garry Horse" (official lineage)

red-river-valley.text: Red River Valley is heard in John Ford's 1940 film of The Grapes of Wrath.
red-river-valley.source: Film Forum, "The Grapes of Wrath" (program note)

home-on-the-range.text: In 1908 the folk song collector John Lomax recorded a saloon keeper singing it, a man who had once driven cattle up the Chisholm Trail.
home-on-the-range.source: Kansas Historical Society, Kansapedia, "Home on the Range"

home-on-the-range.text: In 1934 an Arizona couple sued for $500,000, saying it copied their own song, My Arizona Home. Their claim was rejected.
home-on-the-range.source: Kansas Historical Society, Kansapedia, "Home on the Range"

home-on-the-range.text: In 1933 President Franklin D. Roosevelt named it his favorite song.
home-on-the-range.source: Kansas Historical Society, Kansapedia, "Home on the Range"
